response.goal: Move audit-report generation out of the HTTP request path while preserving durable work, limiting repeated computation, and making failures diagnosable by operators.
response.current_state: The Node.js monolith generates reports synchronously during customer HTTP requests. Generation takes 20 seconds to 4 minutes, leading to timeouts and repeated work when clients retry.
constraints: PostgreSQL remains the source of truth.
Redis is intended for ephemeral caching today.
No new managed service can be adopted this quarter.
Accepted report requests must not be lost.
Duplicate delivery is tolerable only when recorded.
Operators must be able to determine why a report failed.
The solution must be practical for a two-engineer team.
assumptions: The team may add PostgreSQL tables, indexes, and worker processes within the existing monolith deployment.
Report creation can be represented by stable input parameters and a unique request or idempotency key.
Returning HTTP 202 with a report identifier and exposing report status or retrieval endpoints is acceptable to clients.
The existing PostgreSQL deployment has enough headroom for an initially bounded worker workload; this must be measured.
Exactly-once execution is unnecessary; durable at-least-once processing with recorded attempts and deliveries satisfies the requirement.

alternatives.name: Keep synchronous generation with mitigations
alternatives.tradeoffs: Add idempotency keys, persist request state, increase HTTP timeouts where possible, and cache completed reports. This is the smallest change and can reduce repeated work, but long computation remains coupled to client connections, deployments, and request-serving capacity. It does not reliably solve timeout behavior across clients and proxies.
alternatives.contraindications: Contraindicated when work commonly exceeds infrastructure or client timeout limits, when retries must not trigger concurrent generation, or when report execution must survive HTTP-process restarts.

alternatives.name: PostgreSQL-backed durable job table and worker
alternatives.tradeoffs: Persist each report request, state, attempts, lease/lock information, failure details, and delivery records in PostgreSQL. A worker in the existing codebase claims jobs using short transactions and PostgreSQL row-locking semantics such as FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then performs generation outside the transaction. This uses the existing source of truth, supports atomic request-and-job creation, durable retries, idempotency, and operator-visible history. Costs include schema and worker lifecycle work, careful lease recovery, bounded retry policy, cleanup, observability, and additional database load.
alternatives.contraindications: Contraindicated if measurement shows PostgreSQL cannot absorb queue polling, state transitions, or report-query load without harming transactional traffic; if throughput requires queue features the small team cannot safely build; or if jobs cannot be made idempotent or protected by leases.

alternatives.name: Redis-backed queue
alternatives.tradeoffs: A Redis queue library may provide convenient workers, retries, scheduling, and concurrency controls. However, Redis is currently used for ephemeral caching, so durable acceptance would depend on persistence, replication, eviction, backup, and recovery guarantees that are not established in the supplied facts. Coordinating durable job state with PostgreSQL also introduces a dual-write failure boundary unless PostgreSQL first records the request and an outbox reliably publishes it to Redis.
alternatives.contraindications: Contraindicated when accepted work must not be lost but Redis durability and non-eviction are not explicitly operated and tested, or when the team cannot maintain an outbox/reconciliation path between PostgreSQL and Redis. It becomes reasonable if Redis is separately configured and operationally supported as a durable queue and load testing rules out PostgreSQL queueing.

evidence.claim: Report generation currently executes inside the HTTP request.
Report generation takes between 20 seconds and 4 minutes.
The current design causes request timeouts and repeated work when clients retry.
PostgreSQL is the source of truth, while Redis is already used for ephemeral caching.
The team cannot adopt a new managed service this quarter.
Accepted reports must not be lost, duplicate delivery is tolerable if recorded, and operators need failure explanations.
A PostgreSQL job record can be committed atomically with report-request state, avoiding a database-to-queue dual-write gap.
The current Redis role does not establish the durability guarantees required for accepted jobs.
A PostgreSQL worker is likely the lowest-operational-complexity durable option for this team, provided database headroom is validated.

response.recommendation: Adopt a PostgreSQL-backed report-job design as the next architectural step. On request, atomically create or reuse a report request keyed by an idempotency key, persist a pending job, and return HTTP 202 with its identifier. Run a bounded worker that claims jobs with a renewable lease, records every attempt and structured failure reason, retries only classified transient failures with limits, and marks exhausted jobs failed. Store an immutable delivery-attempt record before or alongside each delivery action so duplicates are visible. Keep report generation and delivery idempotent where possible. Provide operators with job state, timestamps, attempt history, lease ownership, error classification, and correlation identifiers. Do not use Redis as the authoritative queue unless its durability model is deliberately changed and tested.
response.expected_gain: HTTP requests should become short-lived acknowledgements rather than report-generation sessions; client retries should converge on the same persisted request; accepted work should survive application restarts; and operators should gain a durable explanation of attempts, failures, and duplicate deliveries. The magnitude of latency, capacity, and reliability improvement should be measured during validation rather than predicted.
response.validation_experiment: Implement a reversible, narrow pilot behind a feature flag for internal users or a small report-type cohort. Add the job and attempt tables, one worker with strict concurrency limits, idempotent request handling, lease expiry, and operator-readable failure records. Keep the synchronous path available for rollback. Exercise success, process termination during generation, lease recovery, transient and permanent failures, repeated client submissions, deployment restart, and duplicate delivery recording. Measure queue age, claim latency, completion time, retry counts, duplicate computation, PostgreSQL load and lock contention, and impact on normal transactions. Expand only if accepted jobs are recovered correctly and database impact stays within existing operational limits; otherwise disable the flag and evaluate a durable Redis configuration with a PostgreSQL outbox.
risks: Queue polling and report queries may increase PostgreSQL load or lock contention.
Incorrect lease handling can leave jobs stuck or cause concurrent execution.
Retries can amplify load unless errors are classified, attempts are bounded, and backoff is applied.
Database migrations and worker deployment could create compatibility issues during rollout.
Storing detailed errors may expose sensitive report data unless messages are sanitized and access-controlled.
Job, attempt, and delivery history require retention and cleanup policies.
A PostgreSQL queue may become unsuitable if future workload scale or scheduling requirements grow substantially.
response.reversibility: High for the proposed pilot: it is additive, cohort-controlled, and leaves the synchronous path intact. Disabling job admission and draining or reconciling existing jobs restores the prior execution path; additive tables can remain for audit history until a safe later cleanup.

adr_handoff.reason: This decision establishes durable-work semantics, ownership boundaries, failure and retry policy, delivery recording, and a deliberate choice of PostgreSQL over Redis. Those constraints and reconsideration triggers should be preserved for future engineers.
